diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Analysis

The current program is a 16-wide unrolled loop followed by a reslice-and-index tail. The cost is dominated by the per-word work: every `xs[i]` in the hot loop needs a bounds check, an index address computation, and a load. Those are the SSA instructions I want to cut.

**Proposed change: index the 16-word block through an array pointer.** `(*[16]uint64)(xs)` is a single conversion, with one length check per block. After it, `a[0]` through `a[15]` are constant-offset loads from one base pointer, so the bounds checks and per-element `IndexAddr` ops go away. The loop condition `len(xs) >= 16` still guarantees the conversion won't panic, and `xs = xs[16:]` is unchanged, so the output and the no-mutation requirement are preserved.

**Risk:** the interpreter must support slice-to-array-pointer conversion. If it doesn't, the candidate fails and scores below the current program. If it does, the saving is roughly one bounds check and one index op per word in the hot loop. I'm not certain of the exact gain, so treat this as a candidate to test rather than a guaranteed win.

The tail stays as it is, since it runs at most once per call and its structure is already tight.
